similarOrganizations.name: Youth International Conclave - YIC
similarOrganizations.description:
Youth International Conclave Model United Nations (YICMUN) is an interactive, interdisciplinary simulation which places students in the role of official United Nations delegates. Participants research a country, take on roles as diplomats, investigate international issues, debate, deliberate, consult, and then develop solutions to world problems.

YICMUN avails students the opportunity to gain first-hand experience in public speaking, negotiation, bargaining, critical thinking, problem solving, lobbying and leadership and helps to build a stronger and diverse networks.

YICMUN avails students the opportunity to gain first-hand experience in public speaking, negotiation, bargaining, critical thinking, problem solving, lobbying and leadership and helps to build a stronger and diverse networks.

YICMUN  will focus on areas of peace and conflict resolution that are a part of the day-to-day work of the United Nations. Participants will be delegations representing the positions of assigned countries in the General Assembly, Security Council and numerous other committees. Within the committees the participants assume the role of representatives from their assigned states to debate the chosen topic agenda. Delegates represent the foreign policy of a country and do their best to portray their views to the other members. The debates are held in formal English, and student diplomats have to observe formal and diplomatic procedure.
Before playing out their ambassadorial roles, students research global problems to be addressed, drawn from today’s headlines. Members learn how the international community acts on its concerns about topics concerning peace and security, human rights, the environment, food and hunger, economic development, and globalization. Model UN delegates also look closely at the needs, aspirations and foreign policy of the countries they will represent during the event.

json.name: Artificial Intelligence Community of Pakistan
json.tagline: Evolution to Revolution
json.description:
The Artificial Intelligence (AI) Community of Pakistan aims to work with a wide range of individuals and organizations from academia, industry, and government.

However, in general, the mission of the AI community may include:
- To advance the field of AI through research and development, including developing new algorithms, techniques, and applications for AI.
- To promoting collaboration and communication among researchers, practitioners, and industry leaders in the field of AI.
- To educate the public and policy-makers about the potential benefits and risks of AI and its impact on society.
- To foster responsible and ethical use of AI, including addressing issues such as bias, transparency, and accountability in AI systems.
- Helping to ensure that the development and deployment of AI aligns with the values of society and is beneficial to all.

The AI community of pakistan also looking forward to work with many organizations such as IEEE, IEEE Computer Society, AI Conference, and other AI-focused groups that work on promoting the responsible use of AI and advancing the field of AI.

similarOrganizations.name: Artificial Intelligence Board of America
similarOrganizations.description:
Artificial Intelligence Board of America (ARTiBA), established in 2015, is the world’s first global standards authority for Artificial Intelligence credentialing and academic accreditation.

As an independent, vendor-neutral body, ARTiBA defines structured benchmarks for professional capability and institutional excellence in AI. Its standards architecture is anchored in the AMDEX™ Framework, a comprehensive model governing AI engineering, architecture, risk oversight, ethics, and enterprise transformation.

ARTiBA awards globally recognized professional credentials and accredits academic institutions for standards-aligned AI education.

Its flagship credentials include:

• AiE® (Artificial Intelligence Engineer)
• CaiEP® (Chartered AI Engineering Professional)
• CAiBP® (Chartered AI Business Professional)

Recognized worldwide, ARTiBA credentials and accreditation signal technical rigor, systems-level authority, and responsible AI practice across industries.

Actuarial Consulting has existed for quite a while but is now emerging in Pakistan due to the rise of international clients, usually Takaful firms, but also the conventional insurance market looking our way. This community is eager to welcome like-minded students who are heading towards career trajectories like Takaful/Insurance, Employee Benefits & Consulting.

This discipline usually involves being proficient in Statistics, Finance, Risk Management and many more other diverse specializations that come later, like Data Science, Accounting Frameworks, Quantitative Analysis, Investment Portfolios etc.

You basically climb the ladder through either 1 of the 3 prominent international exam bodies (SOA/CAS/IFOA). They certify you, after clearing a long list of exams (similar to for e.g. ACCA), as an expert in mainly, but not limited to, the different components of the insurance field: Claims Reserving, Pricing, Financial Reporting etc.

Here, you may find helpful LinkedIn posts, links to free exam prep resources, sample projects involving advanced MS Excel, VBA, Macros, as well as programming that actuarial analysts use to automate and make their work more efficient, and sometimes just random advice on how to manage an actuarial career.

At the moment, candidates hoping to attempt SOA's exam P (Probability) soon or in the coming year (2026) can join and practice the Society of Actuaries pattern of questions together, as well as students who would like to collaborate on Excel assignments designed by Casualty Actuarial Society representatives so you could get an idea what this field is all about.
Join to build a network with aspiring actuaries. 

If possible, please also share this page/community link with the math and finance geeks that might find these resources helpful.

Building on its momentum, NSTP has launched the Center for Emerging Technologies (CEMTECH) to accelerate research and application of AI technologies. Additionally, the development of One IT Towers will add 200,000 sq. ft. of premium space dedicated to IT companies, further expanding the park’s capacity to serve as Pakistan’s innovation powerhouse.

If we redraw boundaries and simply reproduce the same centralised decision-making, weak local ownership, and bureaucratic bottlenecks at a smaller scale, we won't have built more capable institutions — we'll have built more administrative units running the same broken operating model. A smaller province with the same command-and-control secretariat culture, the same disconnect between elected representatives and career bureaucracy, and the same weak own-source revenue base isn't reform. It's replication.

This is why costing new provinces can't stop at fiscal arithmetic — what a new secretariat, judiciary bench, or PSC cadre will cost to stand up. It has to include institutional costing: what capacity, what delegated authority, what local ownership structure has to be designed in from day one for the new unit to actually function differently, not just at a smaller radius.

The reforms that outlast a change in government are the ones institutions own from the outset, not the ones imposed from the top and defended by whichever leadership happened to launch them. Applied to the provinces debate, that means any serious proposal should have to answer, upfront:

 → Who holds fiscal autonomy in the new unit, and how is it protected from provincial-style re-centralisation?
 → How is local recruitment and PSC design structured to build institutional memory, not just replicate transferred staff?
 → What decision rights are genuinely delegated, versus retained at the centre under a different letterhead?

Redrawing the map is the easy, visible part of this reform. Redesigning how institutions behave inside the new lines is the part that actually determines whether it works.

Gulbaz Ali Khan 
CEO, Analytics Lab Pakistan

As someone who has spent years working on public sector governance reforms across Pakistan, I'll say it plainly: administrative restructuring is necessary. Federal Minister Aleem Khan has openly backed separate Hazara, South Punjab and Bahawalpur provinces, and gone further: proposing that each of the four existing provinces be split into four administrative units. MQM-P is calling for a formal national dialogue on the framework. PTI has endorsed the principle too. This isn't a fringe idea — it's a governance necessity. Pakistan's provinces are too large, too distant from the districts they govern, and too centralised for effective service delivery. Punjab alone still administers over 110 million people through a structure designed for a much smaller, less complex province. That mismatch is a real drag on service delivery, and it needs to be fixed.

Smaller, better-designed units mean:
 → Shorter administrative distance between citizens and decision-makers
 → More responsive local budgeting and service delivery
 → Political representation that better reflects regional identity and development grievances (Saraiki belt, Hazara, interior Sindh)

But necessity doesn't excuse doing it carelessly. The costing has to be treated as a non-negotiable part of the reform, not an afterthought.

Every new province means a new secretariat, a new bureaucratic tier, new PSC cadres, a new High Court bench, new development budgets — layered onto a public financial management system that is already stretched, still digitising, and still struggling with weak own-source revenue mobilisation at the sub-national level. If the transition isn't costed upfront — with clear estimates of setup and recurring administrative expenditure, cost-effective institutional design, shared services where possible, and hard revenue-generation targets for the new units — fragmentation on the map will simply become fragmentation of the budget: more overhead, not more capacity.

So the position I'd put forward is this: new provinces, yes — Pakistan needs them. But every proposal must come with a costed implementation plan before it comes with a resolution.

Reform the map — but cost it first, and cost it honestly.

Gulbaz Ali Khan
CEO, Analytics Lab Pakistan

Within the committees the participants assume the role of representatives from their assigned states to debate the chosen topic agenda. Delegates represent the foreign policy of a country and do their best to portray their views to the other members. Model UN delegates also look closely at the needs, aspirations and foreign policy of the countries they will represent during the event.

similarOrganizations.name: University of Engineering and Technology, Lahore
similarOrganizations.description:
University of Engineering and Technology (UET) Lahore

Founded in 1921 as Mughalpura Technical College and later renamed Maclagan Engineering College in 1923, UET Lahore is one of Pakistan’s oldest and most prestigious engineering institutions. Initially offering programs in Electrical and Mechanical Engineering, it expanded to Civil Engineering by 1947.

Over the decades, UET has grown into a leading hub for engineering, architecture, planning, and allied disciplines. By the 1970s, it had established strong postgraduate and PhD programs, and in 1975, founded its first sub-campus at Taxila.

Located on the historic Grand Trunk Road near the Shalimar Gardens, UET Lahore continues to be a center of academic excellence, innovation, and research, nurturing engineers and technologists for global impact.

similarOrganizations.name: Department of Computer Science | UET Lahore
similarOrganizations.description:
The Department of Computer Science is among the most prestigious and oldest institutions for computer science education in the country. Its origins date back to 1968, when UET Lahore established a Computer Center under the supervision of the Department of Mathematics. The center was equipped with an IBM 1130 third-generation batch processing system, featuring disk storage and monitoring capabilities.

Initially, the center was responsible for delivering courses in Computer Science and Numerical Analysis, which formed an essential component of the B.Sc. Engineering curricula across all disciplines at UET. In addition, it offered short-term computer training programs for both public and private sector organizations.

The department expanded its academic offerings with the introduction of a Bachelor's degree program in Computer Science in 1976. This was further upgraded to a Master’s (MSc) program in 1978, making it the first institution in the country to offer graduate-level education in Computer Science.

In 1991, the Computer Center was formally elevated to an independent Department of Computer Science. The department is further distinguished by holding an endowed chair sponsored by His Majesty Sultan Qaboos Bin Said Al-Said, Sultan of Oman.

At the moment, candidates hoping to attempt SOA's exam P (Probability) soon or in the coming year (2026) can join and practice the Society of Actuaries pattern of questions together, as well as students who would like to collaborate on Excel assignments designed by Casualty Actuarial Society representatives so you could get an idea what this field is all about.

If we redraw boundaries and simply reproduce the same centralised decision-making, weak local ownership, and bureaucratic bottlenecks at a smaller scale, we won't have built more capable institutions — we'll have built more administrative units running the same broken operating model. A smaller province with the same command-and-control secretariat culture, the same disconnect between elected representatives and career bureaucracy, and the same weak own-source revenue base isn't reform. It's replication.

This is why costing new provinces can't stop at fiscal arithmetic — what a new secretariat, judiciary bench, or PSC cadre will cost to stand up. It has to include institutional costing: what capacity, what delegated authority, what local ownership structure has to be designed in from day one for the new unit to actually function differently, not just at a smaller radius.

The reforms that outlast a change in government are the ones institutions own from the outset, not the ones imposed from the top and defended by whichever leadership happened to launch them. Applied to the provinces debate, that means any serious proposal should have to answer, upfront:

 → Who holds fiscal autonomy in the new unit, and how is it protected from provincial-style re-centralisation?
 → How is local recruitment and PSC design structured to build institutional memory, not just replicate transferred staff?
 → What decision rights are genuinely delegated, versus retained at the centre under a different letterhead?

Redrawing the map is the easy, visible part of this reform. Redesigning how institutions behave inside the new lines is the part that actually determines whether it works.

Gulbaz Ali Khan 
CEO, Analytics Lab Pakistan

#PublicFinance #Governance #Pakistan #PFM #ProvincialReform #InstitutionalReform

As someone who has spent years working on public sector governance reforms across Pakistan, I'll say it plainly: administrative restructuring is necessary. Federal Minister Aleem Khan has openly backed separate Hazara, South Punjab and Bahawalpur provinces, and gone further: proposing that each of the four existing provinces be split into four administrative units. MQM-P is calling for a formal national dialogue on the framework. PTI has endorsed the principle too. This isn't a fringe idea — it's a governance necessity. Pakistan's provinces are too large, too distant from the districts they govern, and too centralised for effective service delivery. Punjab alone still administers over 110 million people through a structure designed for a much smaller, less complex province. That mismatch is a real drag on service delivery, and it needs to be fixed.

Smaller, better-designed units mean:
 → Shorter administrative distance between citizens and decision-makers
 → More responsive local budgeting and service delivery
 → Political representation that better reflects regional identity and development grievances (Saraiki belt, Hazara, interior Sindh)

But necessity doesn't excuse doing it carelessly. The costing has to be treated as a non-negotiable part of the reform, not an afterthought.

Every new province means a new secretariat, a new bureaucratic tier, new PSC cadres, a new High Court bench, new development budgets — layered onto a public financial management system that is already stretched, still digitising, and still struggling with weak own-source revenue mobilisation at the sub-national level. If the transition isn't costed upfront — with clear estimates of setup and recurring administrative expenditure, cost-effective institutional design, shared services where possible, and hard revenue-generation targets for the new units — fragmentation on the map will simply become fragmentation of the budget: more overhead, not more capacity.

So the position I'd put forward is this: new provinces, yes — Pakistan needs them. But every proposal must come with a costed implementation plan before it comes with a resolution.

Reform the map — but cost it first, and cost it honestly.

Gulbaz Ali Khan
CEO, Analytics Lab Pakistan

#PublicFinance #Governance #Pakistan #PFM #ProvincialReform #NewProvinces #AdministrativeUnits
